finalResponse:
# Notes Written Before We Commission the Map

*Deliberately before. The moment a consultancy delivers a tiered supplier map with a heat overlay, the question stops being "where are we actually exposed" and becomes "which amber cells shall we turn green" — and the map will be wrong in precisely the places that matter, because the sub-tiers it can see are the ones that answered the survey.*

---

## The framing I'd put down first

The brief describes two programmes: resilience and ethics. I'd resist that from the outset, gently, because they will otherwise be given to two different owners with two different budgets and two different reporting lines, and they will duplicate the same work badly.

They are one problem wearing two coats. Both fail at the same place — tier two and below. Both are defeated by the same thing, which is not knowing who is actually making the part. And increasingly they fail *together*: a forced-labour finding somewhere in the third tier of a spinning mill no longer produces a press cycle, it produces detained goods at a border. Ethical opacity has become a delivery risk with a customs form attached. That's the argument that gets this funded properly, and it happens to be true.

So: one visibility programme, two uses.

## The second thing I'd interrogate before the first

"Recent global events highlighted the need." I'd want to know what they highlighted specifically, and I'd want it in the form of a number rather than a feeling.

The number I'd ask for is unglamorous. For each of our top failure candidates: **if that facility stopped on Friday, when does our line stop, and when could we be shipping again from somewhere else?** Time-to-survive against time-to-recover. Where the second exceeds the first, we have an exposure. Where it doesn't, we have an anxiety, and anxieties are cheaper to leave alone than to fix.

That framing does something useful and slightly subversive: it declines to treat "supply chain risk" as a general condition requiring a general response. Most resilience spending is a tax paid evenly across a book of parts in which the actual fragility is concentrated in perhaps thirty line items, several of which cost under ten pounds and none of which appear on a spend-weighted dashboard. Procurement's attention follows money. Production stoppages follow criticality. Those two lists overlap far less than anyone expects, and the gap between them is where I'd spend the first fortnight.

And the concentration question needs asking one level deeper than it usually is. Three qualified suppliers in three countries is not diversification if all three buy from the same refiner, the same coating house, the same industrial park, the same port, the same single-source proprietary controller. False redundancy is more dangerous than acknowledged single-sourcing, because it has already been signed off.

---

## The error I'd most want to avoid: buying inventory when the thing we need is optionality

Buffer stock is the reflex. It is the most expensive, most perishable and least transferable form of resilience available — it protects against exactly one duration of exactly one disruption, it obsoletes, and it ties up the working capital we'd need to *respond*. Some is right. A general inventory increase across the book is a decision not to think.

What actually confers resilience is optionality, and optionality is mostly bought in three places, none of which sit inside procurement:

**Engineering.** Single-sourcing is usually not a purchasing failure. It's a design decision made three years ago by someone specifying a part number, and it cannot be undone by a buyer, only by a qualification programme. Which means a meaningful share of the resilience budget belongs to R&D: fewer unique parts, wider tolerances, specs written to function rather than to a manufacturer's datasheet, and a **design-review gate that a sole-sourced critical component cannot pass without an explicit, named exception**. That gate is worth more over five years than any amount of dual-sourcing pleading afterwards.

**Contract structure.** Paid capacity options rather than volume commitments. Tooling that we own and can physically locate and move, with the transfer rehearsed rather than asserted. Process documentation in escrow. A right to audit that explicitly reaches sub-tiers. A prohibition on unauthorised subcontracting with a consequence attached that isn't a letter — because unauthorised subcontracting is where both the disruptions and the abuses actually live, and it is nearly always invisible to an announced audit.

**Warm alternates.** A qualified second source with no volume flowing through it decays into an unqualified second source in about eighteen months. Five to ten per cent of the volume, permanently, costs a little on unit price and buys a supplier who is live, current, and has our tooling running. I'd rather pay that than hold the equivalent in stock.

---

## On the ethical side, three things I'd say quietly and mean firmly

**Audits mostly don't work, and we should stop pretending otherwise.** The record is not ambiguous. Announced visits, coached workers, duplicate books, and the sites with the worst conditions are frequently the ones with the cleanest certificates. What carries actual signal: unannounced visits; worker-voice channels that are not administered by the supplier and not routed through the supplier's HR; time-and-attendance records checked against output; and above all the **recruitment corridor** — who the labour agent was, what the worker paid to get the job, and who holds the documents. Debt bondage is the most common serious violation in cross-border manufacturing labour and it is almost never found by inspecting a factory floor. It is found by asking a worker what they paid.

**We cannot demand compliance at a price that mathematically excludes it.** If we hold a five per cent annual cost-down and simultaneously prohibit excessive overtime, we have asked our suppliers for a lie and we will be given a well-formatted one. The cost of legal hours, legal wages and a functioning safety system belongs in the price, stated separately, and protected from the next negotiation. Anything else is outsourcing the violation along with the part.

**And the uncomfortable one: discovery should not automatically trigger exit.** The instinct on finding child or forced labour is to cut the supplier immediately — which is defensible reputationally and frequently worse for the person harmed, who loses income without gaining protection. It also teaches every other supplier that the cost of disclosure is termination, which guarantees we never learn anything again. Remediation first, with a defined plan, funded partly by us, verified independently; exit reserved for *refusal* to remediate or for repeat concealment. I'd want that written down before the first finding, because after the first finding nobody will have the nerve.

Also worth saying plainly: our leverage is a function of what percentage of a supplier's revenue we represent. Where we are two per cent, our code of conduct is correspondence. There the honest routes are shared audit consortia, industry-common standards, or accepting that we're a passenger and pricing that risk rather than papering it.

---

## What I'd actually propose

Sequenced, each stage gated on the one before, because a programme that starts everywhere finishes nowhere.

**First sixty days — criticality, not spend.** Rank every input by what it stops and how fast. Take the top thirty to fifty. For each, name the actual manufacturing site (not the trading entity), the upstream input, the route, and the chokepoint. Where we cannot name it, that is the finding — record the blanks as blanks rather than filling them with the supplier's assurance. Gate: we can state time-to-survive and time-to-recover for the whole critical set.

**Next ninety days — the cheap, unglamorous, available-now layer.** Tooling located and ownership confirmed. Capacity options taken on the three or four genuine chokepoints. Documentation escrowed. Contract clauses on subcontracting and sub-tier access inserted at the next renewal in every case. Faster payment terms for small tier-two suppliers, which is the least fashionable resilience investment available and one of the most effective, since their fragility is our stoppage.

**In parallel, permanently — design.** The sole-source gate. A standing target for unique-part reduction. This is slow and it is the only part of the programme that compounds.

**Then, on evidence — qualification.** Regional alternates for the parts where the first stage proved a real gap, in a different failure basin, kept warm with real volume. Not everywhere. Where the numbers said.

**Ethics, running alongside rather than after.** Worker-voice channel independent of suppliers, in the languages actually spoken on the floor, in the top corridors first. Recruitment-fee audits in the migrant-labour lanes. Unannounced visits replacing a proportion of scheduled ones. Compliance cost isolated in the price. Remediation protocol drafted now, before it's needed.

**Rehearsal, quarterly, from the start.** One tabletop: a named site is gone on Friday, who does what, in what order, with which authority to spend, and what actually breaks. A continuity plan that has never been rehearsed does not exist; it is a document about a plan. This is also where we discover that the person with the authority to release emergency spend is on a different continent and needs three approvals — which is the sort of thing that costs nothing to fix in peacetime and everything in the week it matters.

**And the intervention that makes all of it real:** change what buyers are measured on. A category manager compensated on unit-cost variance will reliably produce concentration, sole-sourcing, opaque tiers and unfunded compliance, and will be right to, because that is what we are paying for. Until dual-source coverage, sub-tier visibility and remediation closure appear in the same scorecard as price, the rest of this is a policy binder. I'd change the scorecard before I'd write the policy.

---

## Walk-away and red-line conditions, fixed now

**Suppliers.** Refusal of sub-tier disclosure on a critical part. Refusal of unannounced access. Evidence of concealment, as distinct from evidence of a violation — the first is disqualifying, the second is a work plan. Retention of worker identity documents. Recruitment fees charged to workers, with no willingness to reimburse. Tooling we own that we are not permitted to inspect.

**Ourselves.** Any resilience measure whose entire content is inventory. Any dual-source claim where the second source converges upstream on the first. Any certificate accepted as evidence where we have not seen the audit methodology and the announcement notice. Any "resilience" line item that survives two budget cycles without being tested against a rehearsal.

**Reshoring.** Not on sentiment. It is a legitimate answer to a specific, quantified exposure and a poor answer to a general unease — and it quietly imports a new single point of failure with a domestic postcode, which we will be slower to see because it looks like ours.

---

## Tests fixed before the map arrives

We can state, for every critical input, the physical site and the upstream input — or we have written down that we cannot.

Time-to-survive and time-to-recover exist as numbers for the critical set.

No critical part is sole-sourced without a dated, named, signed exception.

Compliance cost is a visible, protected line in the price.

A worker in the highest-risk corridor has a way to tell us something without their employer knowing.

The remediation protocol was written before the first finding.

The scorecard changed.

We have run one rehearsal, and something in it failed.

---

The failure mode here isn't a disruption we didn't foresee. It's eighteen months of mapping, a well-designed dashboard, a code of conduct signed by four hundred suppliers, and an organisation that is measurably more documented and not detectably more robust — with everyone reluctant to say so, because the programme has a budget, a champion and a slide.

The defence is the rehearsal. It is the only part of this that cannot be faked, and it is the only part that will tell us, cheaply and in advance, which of our arrangements are real and which are merely written down.
